title: Memory Management Is the New Code
one_liner: Storing memory is solved; a folder in a git repository is the default. The work that remains — keeping memory visible, organised and current — is the interface between human intent and model action, and it has to be maintained like code.
problem: Persisting agent memory is no longer the difficult part. A folder in a git repository already provides a strong default: it is versioned, diffable, reviewable, portable and readable by every agent and every human with a checkout. The harder problems appear after memories accumulate and agents start acting on them. Visibility: a human may not be able to see what the agents currently believe, which pages they actually read, or which decisions are still open. Organisation: an initially clear structure decays as entries, links, copies and one-off documents multiply, and soon nobody knows which page is the entry point. Currency: obsolete guidance remains plausible enough to be recalled, and an out-of-date instruction in a prompt file or decision record steers the next run as confidently as a current one. Once agents do most of the writing and reading, these failures are operational rather than archival: a stale belief produces a wrong action, a duplicated card produces duplicated work, and an invisible decision produces a silent one.
solution: Treat the memory layer as the primary interface between humans and models, and maintain it with the discipline and tooling otherwise reserved for code. Keep durable shared memory as small, addressable files in a dedicated, version-controlled folder: one folder per living document with its own descriptor, one index or entry point per topic complex, one canonical agent-instruction file that every vendor-specific file points to. Give each document an explicit lifecycle state and a place in a visible list, with finished and archived states moved out of the default view but kept readable and linkable. Record decisions inline, next to the analysis that supports them, and record corrections as explicit successors rather than silent rewrites. Let the work that uses a document also maintain it: a task that references a dossier appends its own entry to that dossier's implementation log, and the pipeline refuses the task when the entry is missing or when the log was edited instead of extended; companion sidecars record which tasks touched which page. Measure currency instead of assuming it: band pages by how much code changed since they were last edited, offer an opt-in machine grade with a fingerprint of the graded source, and keep drift reports as first-class documents. Before new work is cut, reconcile the observation against in-flight cards and existing dossiers and record the verdict: covered by an existing key, an operator action that needs no ticket, or a candidate that becomes a card only after a second sighting. Use another store only when a narrow requirement — ephemeral state, high-volume events, cross-repository retrieval at scale, or access controls that git cannot provide — justifies a second place where visibility, organisation and currency can diverge.
